implementation_notes: ServiceLoader.load(Service.class) locates providers declared in META-INF/services/<service> (class path) or by a module's provides directive, instantiates them lazily and caches them per loader; it is the standard component-discovery mechanism, so the Component Repository collapses into a name-keyed map of the configured instances. Discovery is not unlinking: reload() clears the provider cache so new providers are found, but the classes stay loaded, so replacing a component means a fresh class loader and letting the old one become unreachable - use this form when components are present at start-up and reconfiguration is a restart.
pitfalls: ServiceLoader caches provider instances per loader and never unloads classes; reload() only clears the cache, so 'replacing' a provider requires a new class loader whose predecessor becomes unreachable.

Providers are located and instantiated lazily, and failures arrive as ServiceConfigurationError (often thrown from a static initialiser) during iteration rather than at configuration time - validate the configuration eagerly when start-up must fail fast.
On the module path a provider is only found if the module is resolved and reads the service (provides/uses directives); otherwise the component is silently absent from the repository.

variants.name: runtime-defined module layers
variants.implementation_notes: ModuleLayer is the JVM's own answer to linking components into a live process: resolve a Configuration from a ModuleFinder over the component directory against the boot layer, then define a new layer whose modules get their own class loaders; service lookup is layer-aware (ServiceLoader.load(service, layer)), and a layer and its loaders are collectible once unreachable, which is the closest the JVM comes to unlink. The composition is described by module descriptors (requires/provides/exports), so this is the declarative realization; use it when components ship as modules and their dependency versions must be isolated from the application's.
pitfalls: Types loaded in a child layer are not identical to the same classes on the application class path, so the Component contract must live in a parent layer (or the boot layer) or every cast fails.

A layer cannot be undefined: reclaiming it means dropping every reference (modules, loaders, instances, service caches) and letting the GC collect - one static registry is enough to pin it for the life of the JVM.
Each layer duplicates class metadata and class spaces, and a module's exact dependencies must be satisfiable inside the layer or resolution fails before anything is loaded.

variants.name: OSGi bundle life cycle (install/start/stop/update/uninstall)
variants.implementation_notes: An OSGi framework implements the whole pattern: a bundle is the component, its BundleActivator the lifecycle hook, the framework's bundle registry the repository, and the framework itself the configurator, with install, start, stop, update and uninstall operations that really do remove a component from a running VM. Versioned Import-Package/Export-Package declarations add dependency resolution and per-bundle isolation. Choose it when hot deployment and component version independence are requirements and the team accepts a container-managed class loading model and its operational complexity.
pitfalls: A bundle whose imports cannot be resolved stays INSTALLED but never becomes RESOLVED, and the failure is reported through framework events rather than as an exception at the call site - surface the wiring state as part of the repository entry.

Class loading is container-managed: embedded libraries must be listed in Bundle-ClassPath or imported deliberately, and passing the same singleton across bundles is a classic source of class-identity bugs.

OSGi's versioning and service registry only pay off with a container per deployment and a team discipline around package export - otherwise it is a large dependency for what a class loader plus a map would do.
